shows.title: Territorios Inasibles (Ungraspable Territories)
shows.artist: Group show: Lucía Serrano, Axell Guillén, Georgina Flores, and other emerging photographers
shows.dates_note: Hydra's site lists this as its "EXPOSICIÓN ACTUAL" (current exhibition) under the Exposiciones menu, but publishes no opening or closing dates anywhere on the page.
shows.description:
Territorios Inasibles gathers nine emerging photographers around a single, slippery idea: territory not just as physical ground but as the emotional, social, and cultural terrain that shapes how a body moves through the world. Curated by Gabriela González Reyes, the show reads less like a themed survey than a series of overlapping case studies in how photography can register instability — bodily, psychic, geopolitical.

Individual bodies of work swing between registers. One project examines the cultural pressure to ignore physical and emotional distress under a productivity-obsessed culture of self-denial; another turns a critical eye on the hyper-aestheticized, algorithmically consumed body under social media's beauty standards. A more speculative strand mines NASA's Voyager Golden Record for imagery about humanity's imagined contact with alien intelligence, while other series turn inward, toward domestic interiors, inherited family history, and the long aftermath of bodily trauma.

As a Shopify-hosted photography space and bookstore, Hydra has spent a decade building shows out of the students and collaborators who pass through its photobook workshops and production programs, and this show reads as a snapshot of that community rather than a single curatorial thesis — closer to a graduating cohort's group statement than a tightly argued exhibition.

shows.title: Mi bosque es el tianguis, estos injertos son mi lengua (My Forest Is the Tianguis, These Grafts Are My Tongue)
shows.dates_note: Campeche's exhibitions page lists the show's opening as "27 August 2026" under "Current viewing_room" with no closing date published.
shows.description:
Salvador Xharicata's first solo show at Campeche turns the gallery into a kind of dismantled tianguis stall, its market-stall tubing hung with grafted stems of nurite — a plant used in Cherán, Michoacán to calm anxiety and settle the stomach. The artist, who grew up P'urhépecha but largely outside the language itself, uses grafting (the horticultural technique his grandfather used to join peach branches to tejocote trees) as a working metaphor for how identity persists by taking root in something else entirely.

The exhibition mixes watercolors on kozo fiber and pulp paper, carved avocado-wood objects made in collaboration with mask carver Neri Chávez, and assemblages of plaster bandages, second-hand boots, wax and tracing paper. Many pieces literalize the show's title: a fragmented market stall grafted with plant stems, a boot cast in paraffin and beeswax, drawings whose forms visibly erode from one iteration to the next, echoing the way language degrades and mutates across generations.

It's a quiet, materially inventive show about the loss of the P'urhépecha tongue among Xharicata's generation, built less as elegy than as a working demonstration of how something can keep existing by changing shape — a fitting subject for an artist whose own vocabulary comes as much from the tianguis where his parents worked as from the forest his people are known for.

shows.title: Dibujos en papel │ Esculturas (Works on Paper │ Sculptures)
shows.artist: Juan José Gurrola and Danny McDonald
shows.dates_note: Listed as House of Gaga's current Mexico City show on its exhibitions page (curated by Mauricio Marcín); the venue's site does not publish opening or closing dates in the text available to us.
shows.description:
This two-artist pairing puts the late Mexican multidisciplinary artist Juan José Gurrola (1935–2007) — painter, director, and one of the great restless figures of Mexican art of the 1970s and 80s — in dialogue with the American sculptor Danny McDonald, known for uncanny tabletop assemblages built from toy figures, taxidermy-adjacent props, and consumer detritus staged like tiny theater sets.

Gurrola's works on paper here are pastels from the early 1980s and 2000s, loose, gestural, and often verging on caricature — a side of his practice that has been comparatively overlooked next to his film and performance work. Set against these are McDonald's sculptures, glass-cloched tableaux of vinyl toy animals, drips, and pedestal-mounted vignettes that read as darkly comic still lifes about consumption and mortality (one piece is bluntly titled after being "forced to sell artwork from personal collection in order to offset funeral expenses").

Curator Mauricio Marcín, who has worked extensively with the Gurrola archive, sets up a conversation across four decades and two very different sensibilities — Gurrola's loose-handed, satirical draftsmanship and McDonald's obsessively staged miniature worlds — that both artists share a taste for humor sharpened into something more unsettling.

shows.title: Germino – Gemimos – Germinamos
shows.description:
Gabriela Novoa's first solo exhibition in Mexico brings together embroidery and painting built around the Nahua concept of the tunal — the energy said to make dreaming, and connection between people, possible. Losing that energy, in this cosmology, opens the door to illness and depression, and Novoa treats the loss and recovery of it as both a personal and a political subject, rooted in her experience as a Salvadoran artist working through the gendered violence and historical repression of her country.

The work itself is quiet and material rather than didactic: stitched textiles and paintings that draw on native bean plants and other regenerating species as stand-ins for soil, memory, and ancestral care. Novoa treats botany as a language for describing what has been damaged and what can still be grown back, layering a feminist reading of the body onto a set of images that could otherwise pass for straightforward nature studies.

The show is presented in Sala Resquicio, Casa del Lago's platform for emerging practices and counter-narratives outside the standard Latin American canon, curated by Eva Posas. It's a modestly scaled but genuinely personal show, worth a visit for anyone interested in textile-based practice, Central American feminist art, or the ongoing conversation between craft and healing.

shows.title: Yo Solía Ser Uno de Ellos
shows.dates_note: Gallery's own site lists this as its current show (opened as part of GAMA Week, Sept 3-6, 2026) but has not yet posted a closing date on its exhibitions archive.
shows.description:
Tony Solis built his career behind the camera in Mexico City's fashion and editorial world — as founder of Y-Not Mag and an editor at NYLON México — before turning that same eye toward gallery work, and this show is his latest turn as an exhibiting artist rather than image-maker for hire. The title, "I Used to Be One of Them," suggests a reckoning with that earlier professional identity, and with the image industries he spent years working inside.

Solis has a history of pulling from unexpected cultural references — his earlier gallery show riffed on Japanese animation and the music of Tom Waits and Leonard Cohen — and his photographic language tends toward the theatrical and staged rather than observational. Expect a body of new photographic work that reads as personal reckoning dressed in the polish of commercial image-making.

This is a compact solo presentation, opened during GAMA Week 2026, and offers a chance to see how a photographer with deep roots in Mexican fashion media handles more personal, gallery-scaled work.

venue.name: Galería Enrique Guerrero
venue.address: Calle Gral. Juan Cano 103, San Miguel Chapultepec I Sección, Miguel Hidalgo

shows.title: Apnea
shows.description:
Candela Capitán is a dancer and choreographer as much as a visual artist, and her gallery debut at LABOR turns that background into an installation you're meant to move through rather than just look at. Apnea imagines the gallery as a wellness spa from the near future — one where relaxation is achieved by pushing the body to its limits rather than away from them, and where the piece itself only functions when bodies activate it.

The work draws on the history of psychiatric hydrotherapy from the 19th and 20th centuries, using that clinical, sometimes coercive history of "treating" bodies through water and controlled physical states as its conceptual backbone. Capitán's central question — at what point does caring for the body become a way of controlling it — runs through the entire installation, which is designed to stall or pause when the performers holding their breath (the "apnea" of the title) can no longer sustain the piece's rhythm.

It's an unusual first outing for a gallery show: part sculpture, part choreography, and entirely dependent on live bodies to complete it. Worth catching for anyone interested in the overlap between performance art and institutional critique of wellness culture.

shows.title: Hacer Lugar
shows.description:
Studio Lenca is the working alias of Jose Campos, an artist who fled El Salvador's civil war as a small child and crossed Mexico overland with his mother before arriving undocumented in the United States — a journey that sits at the center of this, his first solo exhibition in Mexico. The show's centerpiece is a monumental site-specific mural retracing that route through both memory and imagination, paired with six sculptural figures based on the historiante, the costumed dancers who preserve histories of colonization in El Salvador through performance.

In the adjacent gallery, new paintings sit alongside pieces from Campos's ongoing "Monuments" series — sculptural vessels built from paper and acrylic blankets that turn bureaucratic, utilitarian objects into invented historical artifacts. The through-line across both bodies of work is a rejection of fixed, official narratives about migration and belonging in favor of something more provisional and self-authored.

Campos's work sits in major collections including the Rubell Museum and the Pérez Art Museum, and this show — titled, aptly, "Making Space" — treats space itself as something built collectively rather than simply occupied, a fitting note for an artist whose whole practice is about claiming ground that wasn't necessarily offered.

shows.title: An Obsession with Flowers (Una Obsesión por las Flores)
shows.description:
This group show stages an imagined dialogue between two writers obsessed with flowers from opposite ends of the twentieth century: Marcel Proust, for whom blossoms stood in for memory, class, and desire, and Mario Bellatin, whose 2001 novel "Flowers" pairs each fragment of narrative with a specific bloom. Seventeen international artists — including Iván Argote, Bianca Bondi, Sara Cwynar, Ad Minoliti, Tourmaline, and Kapwani Kiwanga — respond to that literary framework with paintings, wallpapers, ceramics, photographs, sculptures, and installations that use floral imagery as a Trojan horse for less decorative concerns.

The show treats the flower as a genuinely double-edged motif: a critique of colonial extraction in one artist's hands, a meditation on mimetic desire and digital images in another's, a queering gesture or a contemporary vanitas elsewhere. Sara Cwynar's photographic and film work on consumer image culture, Bianca Bondi's installations built from crystallizing and oxidizing materials, and Alberto Perera's Proust-and-Bellatin-inspired wallpaper vignettes give a sense of the range on view — decorative surface used consistently as cover for sharper ideas about desire, power, and representation.

Organized as part of the Gran Fiesta franco-mexicana with support from the French Embassy and a roster of corporate patrons, this is one of the more ambitious group shows on LagoAlgo's calendar this year, and worth seeing for the sheer range of international artists tackling a single, deceptively simple motif.

shows.title: Estados de Inocencia
shows.dates_note: Venue's homepage features this as its current exhibition (with a full catalogue linked) but publishes no opening or closing dates anywhere on the site; outside sources place the opening around late April 2026, still shown as current as of September 2026.
shows.description:
Estados de Inocencia is a survey of paintings and prints by Roger von Gunten, the Swiss-born painter who settled in Mexico in 1957 and became one of the defining voices of the Generación de la Ruptura, the postwar group that turned Mexican art away from muralism's nationalist program toward something more private and imaginative. Von Gunten died in February 2026 at his home in Tepoztlán, so this Polanco presentation reads as a memorial account of a six-decade career rather than a debut.

The works on view move between acrylic paintings and etchings from the 1980s through the 2000s, full of the dreamlike, faintly totemic imagery von Gunten was known for: trees hung with birds, suns and moons rendered as simple glowing discs, enclosed gardens, and shadowy interior scenes that feel closer to folk tale than to observed landscape. Color is used emotionally rather than descriptively, with the kind of loose, saturated brushwork that made him a natural fit alongside Ruptura contemporaries like Gunther Gerzso, Vicente Rojo, and Lilia Carrillo — all artists Óscar Román has long championed.

What makes the show worth a visit is less any single masterpiece than the chance to see how consistent von Gunten's private mythology remained across four decades of work, and to take stock of an artist whose reputation in Mexico (he received the Medalla Bellas Artes in 2014) rests on exactly the kind of quiet, symbol-laden painting this gallery has built its program around.

shows.title: Leaner Mind
shows.dates_note: Lodos' exhibitions page and the show's own page list only "Opening September 3, 2026. Colonia Juárez, Mexico City" with no published closing date.
shows.description:
Isaac De Reza's new solo show at Lodos arrives as the gallery's current presentation in its Colonia Juárez space, following his participation in Lodos' recent group exhibitions "Moving Images" and "Contramundos." De Reza works across sculpture, video and installation, often probing how systems of control — architectural, technological, psychological — shape bodies and behavior, and "Leaner Mind" continues that line of inquiry with a new body of work.

Lodos has built its program on exactly this kind of rigorous, research-driven practice, and De Reza's inclusion alongside gallery peers like Berenice Olmedo and Ghislaine Leung places him in good company. Visitors should expect a tightly focused single-artist presentation rather than a survey — the kind of show this gallery does well, giving one voice room to develop an idea across a full room.

Since the gallery's own page has not yet published a closing date, treat this as an early-in-its-run show: it opened on September 3rd and is very much on view now, but check with Lodos directly if planning a visit toward the end of the season.

shows.title: ¿Cuántas versiones más de mí tienen que morir?
shows.dates_note: Pequod Co.'s exhibitions page lists this show under "Current" with only the opening date 08/28/26; no closing date is published.
shows.description:
Fátima Rodrigo, a Lima-based artist known for sculpture and drawing built from the glitter, sequins and neon of Latin American variety-show television, turns her attention here to Televisa and the telenovela as a machine for producing ideas about femininity. Anchoring the show is a sculpture that reimagines the three-tiered cake from the 1987 teen telenovela "Quinceañera" — silver columns, textured icing rendered as yellow flowers and pink ribbons, a doll in a ruffled gown on top — turning a piece of soap-opera set design into a monument to the sentimental excess the genre is usually mocked for.

A second room shifts from sculpture to works on paper: drawings built from glitches and distortions in the Televisa eye-logo, pulled from home-video footage and corrupted broadcast signals, tracing the network's various rebrandings over the decades. Some stay in black and white; others break into neon cyan, magenta and orange. Under curatorial guidance from Fabiola Iza, the show reads Rodrigo's whole practice as an attempt to find the cracks — the "residual modernism" — inside a supposedly rational, universal visual language, using television's own technical failures as a way in.

It's a smart, tightly argued two-room show for anyone interested in how popular culture, kitsch and gender get worked over in contemporary sculpture, and a good example of the kind of thesis-driven solo presentation Pequod has built its program around.

shows.title: no tenemos caballos para cruzar este caudal
shows.description:
Mariana Paniagua Cortés's first solo show with PEANA, curated by Bruno Enciso, is built from a tight series of mid-size and small canvases worked in acrylic, oil and encaustic — a combination that gives the surfaces a waxy, almost bruised density rather than a flat painterly finish. Titles like "un relámpago significa sí," "el interior de un animal tibio" and "un niño mira por la ventana" point to a recurring cast of half-legible bodies, weather events and domestic interiors that seem to be caught mid-tremor.

The paintings work as a kind of coded weather report for the nervous system: landscape here is not scenery but a membrane that anxiety, premonition and bodily sensation pass through. Paniagua Cortés has spent several years investigating the "metabolic forces of landscape," and this show pushes that inquiry further into the pictorial register, layering encaustic over oil so that some forms look freshly wounded and others already scarred over.

It's a quiet, interior show rather than a spectacular one — best seen slowly, painting by painting, in PEANA's Roma Sur space, itself a former 1940s swimming club. Worth catching before it closes.

shows.title: Música genética
shows.description:
Alan Sierra's upcoming show at PEANA gathers a group of sculptures that fuse the forms of musical instruments with the shapes of everyday tools — objects that look playable but aren't, arranged like an orchestra with no musicians and no sound. It's a continuation of Sierra's long-running interest in the labor behind artistic production, treating the studio's tools and gestures as subject matter in their own right rather than backstage machinery.

Beyond the sculptures, the exhibition includes works that blur the line between drawing and musical notation, plus instrument cases repurposed as game boards, constellations and egg containers — a small, domestic-scale gesture that keeps circling back to ideas of gestation and inherited labor. Sierra frames artistic freedom as something built up over generations rather than a solitary flash of genius, and the show's quietest, most withheld objects make that argument better than any statement could.

shows.title: Flora Intestinal
shows.dates_note: Listed under Salón Silicón's "Exposiciones Actuales / Current Exhibitions" page with no opening or closing date published.
shows.description:
Marina Daiez's Flora Intestinal, curated by Marcela Chao, treats the body as a digestive system for the world's overload of images and stories — something that has to break down, absorb and expel what it takes in just to keep functioning. The paintings and works on paper read like organic diagrams: intestinal, floral and fungal forms tangle together as if composting had become the show's real subject, with flowers literally described as growing out of processed, discarded matter.

Underneath the biological imagery is a show about grief and endings — Daiez imagines a "sick world," governed by extraction and action over care, and sets against it a quieter register of softness, tenderness and attention. Closing one's eyes, in the show's own logic, becomes a small act of resistance in an oversaturated moment.

It's an intimate, tightly curated presentation rather than a spectacle, well suited to Salón Silicón's small Roma Sur project space, and it rewards close looking at the individual works as much as the room as a whole.

shows.title: ¡Que te ruegue quien te quiera!
shows.dates_note: Listed under Salón Silicón's "Exposiciones Actuales / Current Exhibitions" page with no opening or closing date published.
shows.description:
Pablo Bondi paints straight from his phone's camera roll — the show's curatorial text by Germán Paley describes the paintings as built from candid, unposed photos: bar scenes, bodegón still lifes shot over cans of beer, neon signage, backs and torsos, dating-app screenshots, the small unremarkable stuff that ends up defining a life more than any posed picture would. The result is a loose visual diary of queer nightlife in Mexico City rendered in paint, unpolished on purpose.

The cantina recurs as the show's central setting and metaphor: a bar as sanctuary, where older bodies move without needing to perform youth, where cheap decorations and balloon clusters take on the weight of ritual, and where corridos and ballads from the jukebox set the tempo. Bondi's own texts, included alongside the paintings, frame the whole project as an act of archive-diving — going back through his photo roll to recover the feeling of specific nights rather than to document them literally.

It's a warm, unguarded show, more interested in atmosphere and community than in classical composition, and it fits naturally within Salón Silicón's ongoing focus on queer image-making in Mexico City.

shows.title: Asunción Molinos Gordo
shows.dates_note: Venue's own homepage lists the show under CDMX as "Asunción Molinos Gordo · Opening September 3, 2026" (confirmed as the gallery's GAMA Week 2026 opening); no closing date is published yet.
shows.description:
Asunción Molinos Gordo works less like a studio artist than like a field researcher: for two decades she has embedded herself with peasant farmers, agronomists, and rural bureaucracies across Spain, Egypt, Mexico and beyond, turning what she finds there — irrigation logic, seed politics, the paperwork of land tenure — into installation, sculpture, textile, video and sound. Her recurring subject is the small or mid-scale farmer treated not as a picturesque relic but as an intellectual, a keeper of technical knowledge that mainstream ideas of "progress" tend to erase.

This new presentation at Travesía Cuatro's Mexico City space, opening as part of GAMA Week on September 3, brings that research-driven practice to the gallery's Roma Norte townhouse. Coming off a run of major institutional outings — a retrospective at Dubai's Jameel Arts Centre, a survey at Madrid's CA2M, and inclusion in the Guggenheim Bilbao's climate-themed group show Artes de la Tierra — Molinos Gordo arrives with a body of work shaped by sustained attention to land use, food systems and the often-invisible labor that sustains them.

Expect the material vocabulary that has defined her practice: humble, regionally specific materials — clay, jute, ceramic, neon, textile — reworked into objects that carry the weight of agricultural history while resisting easy nostalgia. Her best pieces operate as quiet provocations, asking viewers used to thinking of innovation as urban and digital to reconsider the farmer's plot as a site of equally rigorous knowledge production.

For visitors who know Mexico City's gallery circuit, this is a chance to see how an artist whose reputation has been built largely in European and Gulf institutions translates that research into a commercial gallery context, in a city whose own rural-urban tensions make her subject matter especially resonant.

venue.name: Travesía Cuatro
venue.address: Calle de Valladolid 35, Roma Nte., Cuauhtémoc, 06700 CDMX
